full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: By this judgment we intend to dispose of 24 Rules. Since point of law involved was the same, we have heard the same together.

2. Petitioners have obtained the Rules calling in question legality, first of the orders made by the respondent No. 1 directing the petitioners to declare the value of their imported merch<u>and</u>ise at an amount which was much higher than the value prevalent at the time of opening of the Letter of Credit <u>and</u> secondly, the legality of the circular dated 3-7-1994 (Annexure E to the Writ Petition No. 1704 of 1994) issued under the signature of the Controller, Customs Evaluation Division, Chittagong fixing ''Indicative value of the merch<u>and</u>ises Crude Degummed Soyabean Oil <u>and</u> unrefined Pump Oil for the purpose of assessment of customs duties.

3. Facts stated in the Writ Petition No. 1704 of 1994, in short, are that petitioner opened Letter of Credit on 25-4-1994 for US$ 4,43,(X)0.00 for import of 1000 metric tons of Crude Degummed Soyabean Oil (CDSO) at the rate of US$ 443 per metric ton C&F Chittagong, that after arrival of the goods at Chittagong Port petitioner through his Clearing <u>and</u> Forwarding Agent submitted Bill of Entry on 22-8-1994 for the purpose of assessment of customs duties at the invoice value for taking delivery of the goods imported; that then the respondent No. 1 by the order dated 12-9-1994 directed the petitioner to declare the value of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise at US$ 574 FOB, which was fixed as the ''Indicative-value'' of the merch<u>and</u>ise by the Memo dated 3-7-1994 <u>and</u> also to show separately the freight paid for the purpose of assessment of customs duties.

4. Petitioner being aggrieved by the aforesaid order of the Respondent No. 1 moved this court <u>and</u> has obtained the Rule.

5. Facts stated in Writ Petition No. 2304 of 1994, in short, are that petitioner opened the Letter of Credit on 16-4-1994 for US$ 7,08,000.00 for import of 2000 metric tons of Crude Palm Oil (CPO) at US$ 354 per metric ton C&F Chittagong; that after arrival of the goods petitioner through his Clearing <u>and</u> Forwarding Agent submitted Bill of Entry bearing receiving No. 1459 <u>and</u> 9109 dated 4-10-1994 <u>and</u> 29-11-1994 respectively for assessment of customs duties taking the invoice value at US$ 354 per metric ton <u>and</u> then the respondent No. 1 by the order dated 28-11-1994 <u>and</u> 29-11-1994 (Annexure G <u>and</u> G-1 to the Petition) directed the petitioner to declare the value of the merch<u>and</u>ise at US$ 542 per metric ton FOB which was fixed as ''indicative value'' by the Memo dated 3-7-1994 circulated under the signature of the Controller, Customs Evaluation Division, Chittagong <u>and</u> also to show separately the freight paid.

6. Petitioner being aggrieved by the said action of the respondent No. 1 moved this court <u>and</u> has obtained the Rule.

7. Facts stated in Writ Petition No. 2305 of 1994, on short, are that petitioner opened letter of credit on 16-4-1994 for US$ 2,7,37,128.00 for import of 7,7032 metric tons of Crude Palm Olien (CPO) at US 354 per metric ton C & F Chittagong, that after arrival of the goods petitioner through his Clearing <u>and</u> Forwarding Agent submitted Bills of Entry bonded bearing receiving No. 6826 <u>and</u> 7493 dated 23-11-1994 <u>and</u> 24-11-1994 respectively for assessment of customs duties taking invoice value at US$ 354 per metric ton <u>and</u> then the respondent No. 1 directed the petitioner on 26-11-1994 to declare the value of the merch<u>and</u>ise at US$ 542 per metric ton which was fixed as ''indicative value'' through the circular dated 3-7-1994 issued under the signature of the Controller, Customs Evaluation Division, Chittagong <u>and</u> also to show separately the freight paid.

8. Petitioner being aggrieved by the said action of the respondent No. 1 moved this court <u>and</u> has obtained the Rule.

9. Facts stated in the Writ Petition No. 1935 of 1994, in short, are that petitioner opened the Letter of Credit on 25-4-1994 for US$ 3,54,000.00 to import 1000 metric tons of Crude Palm Oil (CPO) at the rate of US$ 354 per metric ton, C&F Chittagong, that after arrival of the goods petitioner submitted Bill of Entry bearing receiving No. 1199 dated 4-10-1994 through his Clearing <u>and</u> Forwarding Agent for assessment of customs duties <u>and</u> other levies on the basis of invoice value at US$ 354 per metric ton <u>and</u> then the respondent No. 1 by the order dated 4-10-1994 directed the petitioner to declare the value of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise at US$ 542 per metric ton FOB which was fixed as ''Indicative value'' by the circular dated 3-7-1994 for the purpose of assessment of customs duties <u>and</u> that also to declare separately the freight paid.

10. Petitioner being aggrieved by the said action of the respondent No. 1 moved this court <u>and</u> has obtained the Rule.

11. Facts stated in Writ Petition No. 1564 of 1994, in short, are that petitioner opened Letter of Credit on 24-4-1994 for US$ 6,60,000.00 to import 1500 metric tons of Crude Degummed Soyabean Oil (CDSO) at US$ 440 per metric ton C&F Chittagong, that out of the total quantity of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise petitioner got 100 metric tons released on payment of customs duties on the basis of invoice value upon furnishing bank Guarantee in respect of duties realizable in case of assessment of customs duty on the basis of any amount other than the invoice value; that after arrival of the balance quantity of imported merch<u>and</u>ise petitioner submitted Bill of Entry bearing receiving No. 7146 dated 28-4-1994 through his Clearing <u>and</u> Forwarding Agent for assessment of customs duties on the basis of invoice value at US$ 440 per metric ton <u>and</u> then the respondent No. 1 by the order dated 30-8-1994 directed the petitioner to declare the value of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise at US$ 574 per metric ton FOB which was fixed as ''indicative value'' by the memo dated 3-7-1994 circulated under the signature of the Controller of Customs Evaluation Division, Chittagong <u>and</u> also to show separately the freight paid for the purpose of assessment of customs duty.

12. Petitioner being aggrieved by the said action of the respondent No. 1 moved this court <u>and</u> has obtained the Rule.

13. Facts stated in the Writ Petition No. 1172 of 1994, in short, are that petitioner opened Letter of Credit on 4-5-1994 for US$ 4,42,000.00 for import of 1000 metric tons of Crude Degummed Soyabean Oil (CDSO) at US$ 442 per metric ton C&F Chittagong that after arrival of the goods petitioner through his Clearing <u>and</u> Forwarding Agent submitted Bill of Entry No. 9292 <u>and</u> 9293 dated 29-6-1994 for the purpose of assessment of customs duty <u>and</u> other levies taking the invoice value at US$ 442 per metric ton for taking delivery of the goods <u>and</u> then the respondent No. 1 by the order dated 12-7-1994, at Annexure-E <u>and</u> E-1, directed the petitioner to declare the value of the merch<u>and</u>ise at US$ 574 per metric ton FOB which was fixed as'' indicative value'' by the Memo dated 3-7-1994 circulated under the signature of the Controller, Customs Evaluation Division, Chittagong <u>and</u> also to show separately freight paid for the purpose of assessment of customs duties.

14. Petitioner being aggrieved by the said order of the Respondent No. 1 moved this court <u>and</u> has obtained this Rule.

15. Facts stated in Writ Petition No. 1155 of 1994, in short are that, petitioner opened Letter of Credit on 25-4-1994 for US$ 6,63,000.00 for import of 1500 metric tons of Crude Degummed Soyabean Oil (CDSO) at US$ 442 per metric ton C&F, Chittagong that after arrival of 100 metric tons out of the total quantity of 15000 metric tons petitioner submitted import papers for assessment of customs duty <u>and</u> other levies on the same <u>and</u> then the respondent No. 1 by the order dated 4-7-1994 directed the petitioner to declare the value of the goods at US$ 574 per metric ton FOB which was fixed as ''indicative value'' by the circular dated 3-7-1994 circulated under the signature of Controller, Customs Evaluation Division, Chittagong <u>and</u> also to show separately freight paid for the purpose of assessment of customs duties.

16. Petitioner being aggrieved by the said order of the Respondent No. 1 moved this court <u>and</u> has obtained the Rule.

17. Facts stated in Writ Petition No. 1536 of 1994,in short, are that petitioner opened Letter of Credit on 26-5-1994 (28-5-1994) for US$ 4,42,000.00 for import of 1000 metric tons of Crude Degummed Soyabean Oil (CDSO) at US$ 442 per metric ton C&F Chittagong; that after arrival of the goods petitioner through his Clearing <u>and</u> Forwarding Agent submitted Bill of Entry bearing receiving No. 6227 dated 25-8-1994 for assessment of customs duty taking the invoice value at US$ 442 per metric ton; that then the customs authority upon refusing to assess customs duty taking the invoice value as the basis of assessment of customs duty directed the petitioner to declare the value of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise at US$ 574 FOB which was fixed by the circular dated 3-7-1994 circulated under the signature of the Controller, Customs Evaluation Division Chittagong by the order dated 25-8-1994 <u>and</u> that also to show separately freight paid (Annexure-F to the petition) for the purpose of assessment of customs duties.

18. Petitioner being aggrieved by the order of the customs authority moved this court <u>and</u> has obtained the Rule challenging the legality of the order so made.

19. Facts stated in the Writ Petition No. 1391 of 1994 in short, are that petitioner opened Letter of Credit on 25-4-1994 for US$ 8,86,00 for import of 2000 metric tons of Crude Degummed Soyabean Oil (CDSO) at the rate of US$ 443 per metric ton C&F Chittagong; that after arrival of the goods petitioner submitted Bill of Entry bearing receiving Nos. 7722, 7723 <u>and</u> 7786 dated 26-6-1994 for assessment of customs duties <u>and</u> other levies taking invoice value of US$ 443 per metric ton; that the customs authority instead of doing so directed the petitioner to declare the value of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise at US$ 574 per metric ton FOB by the order dated 18-7-1994 which was fixed by the circular dated 3-7-1994 circulated under the signature of the Controller, Customs Evaluation Division, Chittagong <u>and</u> also to show separately the freight paid for the purpose of assessment of customs duties <u>and</u> other levies.

20. Petitioner being aggrieved by <u>and</u> dissatisfied with the order so made by the customs authority moved this court <u>and</u> has obtained the Rule.

21. Facts stated in Writ Petition No. 1561 of 1994, in short, are that, petitioner opened Letter of Credit on 9-5-1994 for US$ 3,53,600 for import of 800 metric tons of Crude Degummed Soyabean Oil in bulk (CDSO) at the rate of US$ 442 per metric ton C&F Chittagong; that after arrival of the goods petitioner through his Clearing <u>and</u> Forwarding Agent submitted Bill of Entry bearing receiving No. 6264 dated 25-8-94 for assessment of customs duty taking invoice value at US$ 442 per metric ton that the customs authority instead of doing so by the order dated 30-8-1994 (Annexure F to the petition) directed the petitioner to declare the value of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise at US$ 574 per metric ton FOB which was fixed by the circular dated 3-7-1994 circulated under the signature of the Controller, Customs Evaluation Division, Chittagong <u>and</u> also to show separately the freight paid for the purpose of assessment of customs duty.

22. Petitioner being aggrieved by the said action of the Customs authority moved this court <u>and</u> has obtained the Rule.

23. Facts stated in Writ Petition No. 1583 of 1994, in short, are that petitioner opened Letter of Credit on 27-4-1994 for US$ 1,32,6,000.00 for import of 3000 metric tons of Crude Degummed Soyabean Oil at the rate of US$ 442 per metric ton C&F Chittagong, that after arrival of the goods petitioner through his Clearing <u>and</u> Forwarding Agent submitted Bills of Entry bearing receiving No. 5306 <u>and</u> 5308 dated 22-8-1994 for the purpose of assessment of customs duties taking the invoice value at US$ 442 per metric ton; that the customs authority instead of doing so directed the petitioner by the order dated 3-9-1994 (Annexure F <u>and</u> F-1 to the petition) to declare the value of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise at US$ 574 FOB, which was fixed by the memo dated 3-7-1994 circulated under the signature of the Controller, Customs Evaluation Division, Chittagong <u>and</u> also to show separately the freight paid for the purpose of assessment of customs duties <u>and</u> other levies.

24. Petitioner being aggrieved by the said action of the customs authority moved this court <u>and</u> has obtained the Rule.

25. Facts, stated in Writ Petition No. 2105 of 1994, in short, are that petitioner opened Letter of Credit on 25-4-1994 for US$ 3,54,000.00 for import of 1000 metric tons of Crude Palm Oil (CPO) at the rate of US$ 354 per metric ton C&F Chittagong, that after arrival of the goods the petitioner through his Clearing <u>and</u> Forwarding Agent submitted Bill of Entry being receiving No. 936 dated 3-11-1994 for assessment of customs duties of the imported goods taking the invoice value at US$ 354 per metric ton, that the customs authority instead of doing so directed the petitioner by the order dated 8-11-1994 (Annexure-F to the Petition) to declare the value of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise at US$ 542 FOB, which was fixed by the circular dated 3-7-1994 circulated under the signature of Controller, Customs Evaluation Division, Chittagong <u>and</u> also to show separately the freight paid for the purpose of assessment of customs duties <u>and</u> other levies.

26. Petitioner being aggrieved by the said action of the customs authority moved this court <u>and</u> has obtained this Rule.

27. Facts stated in Writ Petition No. 1425 of 1994, in short, are that petitioner opened Letter of Credit on 11-4-1994 for US$ 3,54,000 for import of 1000 metric tons of Crude Degummed Soyabean Oil (CDSO) at US$ 354 per metric ton C&F Chittagong, that after arrival of the goods petitioner through his Clearing <u>and</u> Forwarding Agent submitted Bill of Entry (for bond) bearing receiving No. 2934 (Annexure-E to the petition) on 11-6-1994, that thereafter for taking delivery of the 700 metric tons of imported merch<u>and</u>ise from the bonded tank petitioner submitted Bill of Entry being No. 3424 (Annexure-E-1 to the petition) dated 11-6-1994 for assessment of customs duties <u>and</u> other levies, that the customs authority assessed customs duties <u>and</u> other levies at Taka 700594 of the said quantity of the merch<u>and</u>ise in the light of the invoice value; that petitioner on payment of the said amount on 12-6-1994 took delivery of 700 metric tons of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise; that thereafter petitioner submitted Bill of Entry bearing receiving No. 3700 dated 14-8-1994 for assessment of customs duty in respect of the balance quantity of 300 metric tons of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise taking invoice value at US$ 354 per metric ton; that the customs authority upon refusing to assess customs duty on the said 300 metric tons of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise on the basis of invoice value directed the petitioner by the order dated 14-8-1994 (Annexure-G to the petition) to declare the value of the merch<u>and</u>ise at US$ 574 per metric ton FOB, which was fixed by the circular dated 3-7-1994 circulated under the signature of the Controller, Customs Evaluation Division, Chittagong, <u>and</u> that also to show separately the freight paid for the purpose of assessment of customs duties.

28. Petitioner being aggrieved thereby moved this court <u>and</u> has obtained the Rule.

30. Petitioner being aggrieved by the said action of the respondent moved this court <u>and</u> has obtained the Rule.

32. Petitioner being aggrieved by the said action of the Customs authority moved this court <u>and</u> has obtained the Rule.

33. Facts stated in Writ Petition No. 1163 of 1994, in short, are that petitioner opened Letter of Credit on 16-4-1994 for US$ 7,00,800 for import of 2000 per metric tons of Crude Palm Olien (CPO) at US$ 354 per metric ton C& F Chittagong, that after arrival of the goods petitioner submitted Bill of Entry (bond) being receiving No. 5081 <u>and</u> accordingly the goods were stored on 9-5-1994 at customs bonded terminal; that petitioner''s clearing <u>and</u> Forwarding Agent submitted ex-bond Bill of Entry for release of 2000 metric tons of imported merch<u>and</u>ise <u>and</u> the same was received by the customs authority against receiving No. 3302 dated 11-6-1994, that the customs authority refused to assess customs duties in respect of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise taking the invoice value at US $ 354 per metric ton C&F Chittagong; that petitioner''s Customs Agent submitted another ex-bonded Bill of Entry <u>and</u> the same was received by the customs authority against receiving No. 936 dated 4-7-1994 for release of the balance quantity of 800 metric tons; that the customs authority instead of assessing customs duties taking the invoice value at US$ 354 per metric ton directed the petitioner by the order dated 14-7-1994 (Annexure-J to the petition) to declare the value of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise at US$ 542 per metric ton FOB which was fixed by the circular dated 3-7-1994 circulated under the signature of the Controller, Customs Evaluation Division, Chittagong, <u>and</u> that also to show separately the freight paid for the purpose of assessment of customs duties.

34. Petitioner being aggrieved by the said action of the customs authority moved this court <u>and</u> has obtained the Rule.

35. Facts stated in Writ Petition No. 1730 of 1994, in short, are that petitioner opened Letter of Credit on 27.71994 for US$ 1,1,50.000.00 for import of 2000 metric tons of Crude Degummed Soyabean (CDSO) in bulk at US$ 575 per metric ton C& F Chittagong that after arrival of the goods petitioner through his Clearing <u>and</u> Forwarding Agent submitted Bill of Entry being receiving No. 5681 dated 20-9-1994 (Annexure-F to the petition) for assessment of customs duties taking the invoice at US $575 per metric ton, but the customs authority instead of doing so directed the petitioner to declare the value of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise at US $ 585 per metric ton FOB which was fixed by the Customs Group Nathi No.198-AP/Group-8/1994-95 <u>and</u> that also to show separately the freight paid for the purpose of assessment of customs duties.

Facts stated in Writ Petition No. 1429 of 1994, in short, are that the petitioner opened Letter of Credit on 9-9-1993 for import of 3000 metric tons of Crude Degummed Soyabin Oil (CDSO) at the rate of US $ 452 per metric ton C&F Chittagong that out of the total quantity of the said goods 2240 arrived at the Port <u>and</u> petitioner got released of the same on payment of customs duties <u>and</u> other levies assessed taking the invoice value at the rate of US $ 452 per metric ton C&F Chittagong; that on 29-6-1994 the letter of credit was amended for further 2000 metric tons of merch<u>and</u>ise at the rate of US $ Dollar 442 per metric ton C&F Chittagong, that 1000 metric tons out of the total quantity of 200 metric tons as per revised Letter of Credit was shipped by the vessel Throstreah, that before arrival of the goods the customs authority through the circular dated 3-7-1994 issued under the signature of the Controller, Customs Evaluation Division, Chittagong fixed ''indicative value'' of the Crude Degummed Soyabean Oil at US $ 574 per metric ton for the purpose of assessment of customs duties, that petitioner submitted Bills of Entry being receiving No.4090 <u>and</u> 4091 dated 16-8-1994 for assessment of customs duties of the goods imported through the revised Letter of credit taking the invoice value at US $ 442 per metric ton; that the Customs authority instead of doing so by the credited 16-8-1994 (Annexure-F <u>and</u> F-1 to the petition) directed the petitioner to declare the value of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise at US $ 574 per metric ton FOB which was fixed through the circular dated 3-7-1994 <u>and</u> that also to show separately the freight paid for the purpose of assessment of customs duties <u>and</u> other levies.

38. Petitioner being aggrieved by the said action of the respondents moved this court <u>and</u> has obtained the Rule.

39. Facts stated in the Writ Petition No 1845 of 1994, in short, are that petitioner opened Letter of Credit on 3-8-1994 for US $ 1,17,000.00 for import of 2000 metric tons of Crude Degummed Soyabean Oil (CDSO) at the rate of US$ 585 per metric ton C&F Chittagong, that after arrival of the goods petitioner submitted Bills of Entry being receiving No.187 dated 20-9-1994 for assessment of Customs duties taking the invoice value at US $ 585 per metric ton; that the customs authority instead of doing so directed the petitioner by the order dated 17-10-1994 (Annexure-F to the petition) to declare the value of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise at US $ 595 per metric ton in the light of the circular dated 3-7-1994 circulated under the signature of the Controller, Customs Evaluation Division, Chittagong <u>and</u> that also to show separately, the freight paid for the purpose of assessment of customs duties <u>and</u> other levies.

40. Petitioner being aggrieved by the said order of the customs authority moved this court <u>and</u> has obtained the Rule.

41. Facts stated in Writ Petition No.2014 of 1994, in short, are that petitioner opened Letter of Credit on 27-7-1994 for import of 3500 metric tons of Crude Degummed Soyabean Oil at the rate of US $ 575 per metric ton C&F Chittagong, that after arrival of the goods petitioner through his Customs House Agent submitted Bill of Entry (bond) being receiving No.965 dated 3-11-1994 for assessment of customs duties taking the invoice value at US $ 575 per metric ton; that the customs authority instead of doing so directed the petitioner by the order dated 3-11-1994 (Annexure-F to the petition) to declare the value of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise at US $650 per metric ton FOB, which was fixed by the circular dated 3-7-1994 <u>and</u> that also to show separately the freight paid for the purpose of assessment of customs duties <u>and</u> other levies.

42. Petitioner being aggrieved by the action of the respondents moved this court <u>and</u> has obtained the Rule.

43. Facts stated in Writ Petition No. 2296 of 1994, in short, are that petitioner opened letter of Credit on 12-9-1994 for import of 1500 metric tons of Crude Degummed Soyabean Oil (CDSO) at the rate of US $ 585 per metric ton C & F Chittagong; that after arrival of the goods petitioner submitted Bill of Entry (bond) being receiving No.8609 dated 30-10-1994 for assessment of customs duties taking the invoice value at US $ 585 per metric ton; that the customs authority instead of doing so by the order dated 28-11-1994 (Annexure F to the Petition) directed the Petitioner to declare value of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise at US $ 678 per metric ton FOB which was fixed by the Collector of Customs through Nathi No.281- AP/Group-8/94-95 <u>and</u> that also to show separately the freight paid for the purpose of assessment of customs duties <u>and</u> other levies.

44. Petitioner being aggrieved by the action of the respondents moved this court <u>and</u> has obtained the Rule.

45. Facts stated in writ Petition No. 2297 of 1994, in short, are that petitioner opened letter of Credit on 15-9-1994 for import of 1500 metric tons of Crude Degummed Soyabean Oil (CDSO) at the rate of US $ 585 per metric ton C&F Chittagong; that after arrival of the goods petitioner submitted Bill of Entry (bond) being receiving No.8641 dated 30-10-1994 for assessment of customs duties taking the invoice value at US $ 585 per metric ton; that the customs authority instead of doing so directed the petitioner to declare the value of the merch<u>and</u>ise at US $ 670 per metric ton FOB, which was fixed by the order dated 28-11-1994 in Group Nathi No. 281/AP/Group-8/94-95/788-Cus <u>and</u> that also to show separately the freight paid for the purpose of assessment of customs duties.

46. Petitioner being aggrieved by the said action of the respondents particularly customs authority, moved this court <u>and</u> has obtained the Rule.

47. Facts stated in Writ Petition No 2012 of 1994, in short, are that petitioner opened Letter of Credit on 1-9-1994 for import of 3000 Crude Degummed Soyabean Oil (CDSO) at the rate of US $ 585 per metric ton C&F, Chittagong that after arrival of the goods petitioner submitted Bill of Entry (bond) being receiving No.673 dated 23-11-1994 for assessment of customs duties taking the invoice at US $ 585 per metric ton, but the respondent No.1 instead of doing so directed the petitioner by the order dated 3-11-1994 (Annexure-F to the petition) to declare the value of the merch<u>and</u>ise at US $ 595 per metric ton FOB which was fixed by the order of the customs authority made in Nathi No 268/AP/group-8/94-95, <u>and</u> also to show separately the freight paid for the purpose of assessment of customs duties.

49. Facts stated in Writ Petition No.2015 of 1994, in short, are that petitioner opened Letter of Credit on 29-6-1994 for import of 2500 metric tons of Crude Palm Olien at the rate of US $ 354 per metric ton C&F, Chittagong that after arrival of 500 metric tons of the goods out of the total quantity of the merch<u>and</u>ise for which Letter of Credit was opened earlier the petitioner got the same released on the basis of an order passed in Writ Petition No.1663 of 1994; that after arrival of the balance quantity of the goods for which Letter of Credit was opened on 29-6-1994 petitioner submitted Bill of Entry (bond) being receiving No.5340 <u>and</u> 887 dated 18-10-1994 <u>and</u> 3-11-1994 respectively for assessment of customs duties taking the invoice value at US $ 354 per metric ton; that the customs authority instead of doing so directed the petitioner by the order dated 3-11-1994 <u>and</u> 19-10-1994 (Annexure F <u>and</u> F-1 respectively) to declare the value of the merch<u>and</u>ise at US $ 542 per metric ton FOB Chittagong in the light of the order of the Superior officer of the customs <u>and</u> that also to show separately the freight paid for assessment of customs duties <u>and</u> other levies.

50. Petitioner being aggrieved by the said action of the respondents moved this court <u>and</u> has obtained the Rule.

51. Contentions of the petitioners in all the writ petitions are more or less similar. Petitioners have contended that the value that was fixed by the circular being Nathi No APP/Mis./38-94/2127 dated 3-7-1994 (Annexure-E to the writ petition No. 1704 of 1994) <u>and</u> that through the orders made by the customs authority in different 'Nathies' for the purpose of assessment of customs duties were arbitrary <u>and</u> that there was no objective basis in the fixation of the value of the merch<u>and</u>ise imported by the petitioners for the purpose of assessment of customs duties. It has also been contended by the petitioners that National Board of Revenue as well as customs officials in law was not authorized to fix value of a particular imported merch<u>and</u>ise in advance for the purpose of assessment of customs duties, that the customs officials acted illegally in making direction to the petitioners to declare value of their respective merch<u>and</u>ise at a value which the authorities fixed at their level, but not notified through the gazette, that the National Board of Revenue as well as the customs authority acted in a colorable manner in fixing the value of the merch<u>and</u>ise in question in advance for the purpose of assessment of customs duties which in other way was nothing but the tariff value fixed by the authority for assessment of customs duties <u>and</u> as such, the value so fixed having not been notified the action of the respondents of taking the pre-determined non-notified value for assessment of customs duties was illegal that there being no law authorizing the National Board of Revenue as well as customs officials to fix value of any imported merch<u>and</u>ise as ''indicative value'' in advance for the purpose of assessment of customs duties <u>and</u> as such, the action of the respondents in making direction to the petitioners to declare the said'' indicative value'' or that the prefixed value as the value of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise for assessment of customs duties is being treating the petitioner not in accordance with law <u>and</u> consequently being violative of Article 31 of the Constitution, the said action of the respondents is not sustainable in law.

52. Respondent Nos. 2 <u>and</u> 3 have entered appearance <u>and</u> have filed Affidavit-in-opposition in some of the Writ petitions. The Affidavits-in-opposition so filed are similar. The said respondents upon denying the material allegation of arbitrariness, absence of basis <u>and</u> absence of legal sanction in the fixation of the value that has been circulated through the circular dated 3-7-1994 have stated, inter alia, that by the SRO No.XXIV-94/1553/Sulka dated 9-6-1994 tariff value that was notified through the SRO dated 28-10-1993 (Published in the Bangladesh Gazette (Extra-ordinary) dated 1-11-1993) of the Crude Degummed Soyabean Oil ( CDCO) <u>and</u> Crude Palm Olien (CPO) was deleted; that petitioners'' contention that even after deletion of the tariff value the customs authority was required to assess customs duties in the light of the invoice value is not correct; that in the absence of tariff value Government or tax assessing agency is quite competent to fix normal price of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise prevalent in the national <u>and</u> international market, that in fixing the normal value by the tax assessing agency price shown in the invoice is not binding upon the said agency; that the customs authority is competent to assess customs duty in the light of the provisions of section 30 of the Customs Act, 1969; that petitioners'' contention of the circular dated 3-7-1994 fixing ''indicative value'' of CDSO at US $ 574 per metric ton without the approval of the government <u>and</u> that because of non-publication of the said circular in the Gazette the same was not valid is not well founded one in that by the said circular National Board of Revenue has fixed the normal price of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise as per provisions of section 25(1) of the Customs Act, 1969 hereinafter referred to as the Act, <u>and</u> that fixation of normal value need not be published in the official gazette; that question of approval of normal price so fixed by the circular dated 3-7-1994 by the Government is also a misconceived one since the National Board of Revenue as integral part of the Government has fixed the normal price <u>and</u> that the National Board of Revenue is very much empowered by the provisions of section 25(1) of the Act to fix normal price in advance of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise; that petitioners'' claim that the current price of CDSO ranges from US $ 438 to 442 per metric ton is not correct; that for the purpose of determination of normal price of CDSO <u>and</u> CPO respondents through their agencies, particularly through Bangladesh Embassy in Malaysia, collected price of CDSO at US $ 574 per metric ton <u>and</u> that from the price list published in March, 1994 by the United Nations wherein value of the merch<u>and</u>ise has been mentioned at US $ 426 per metric ton FOB <u>and</u> 650 per metric ton FOB in UK <u>and</u> USA respectively <u>and</u> that the respondents also relied upon other materials in fixing the ''indicative value'' of the CDSO; that in fixing the price of CDSO <u>and</u> CPO the authority also took into consideration the interest of the importers, business community <u>and</u> consumers <u>and</u> thereupon fixed the ''indicative value'' of CDSO at US $ 574 per metric ton; that as there was no tariff value when the Bills of Entry were submitted for assessment of customs duties <u>and</u> that invoice value being not binding on the tax assessing agency in the assessment of customs duties <u>and</u> that as the tax assessing agency was quite competent to fix the normal price of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise in the light of the price of the imported goods prevalent in the national <u>and</u> international market <u>and</u> that price of the merch<u>and</u>ise having already been fixed by the National Board of Revenue taking into consideration the price of the imported goods prevalent in the national <u>and</u> international market the customs authority did not commit any illegality in making the directions to the petitioners to declare the value of the merch<u>and</u>ise at the FOB value that was mentioned in the orders made in the body of the Bills of Entry for the purpose of assessment of customs duties <u>and</u> that also to show separately the freight paid for the purpose of assessment of customs duties, that in the fixation of the price by the circular dated 3-7-1994 respondents relied upon the dependable materials collected from different sources including the price mentioned in the oil world magazine, a most dependable magazine which monitors the oil price, including the price of the merch<u>and</u>ise imported by the petitioners, in the international market; that the object of fixing the price through the circular dated 3-7-1997 was to prevent under-invoicing of the value of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise <u>and</u> that in fixing the price so circulated by the circular hereinbefore mentioned the respondents acted quite fairly <u>and</u> reasonably in exercise of their statutory power as in the Act <u>and</u> as such, the price so fixed cannot be said an unlawful one or that it can be said the price so fixed has been fixed without any legal authority;, that petitioners were quite aware of fixation of the price by the Memo dated 3-7-1994 <u>and</u> that as against the said circular petitioners made representations to the National Board of Revenue for reconsideration of the matter of fixation of the value of the, imported merch<u>and</u>ise by the authority described as ''indicative value''; that the petitioners in their representations made to the National Board of Revenue have admitted that some quantity of CDSO they have imported at a rate at US $ 580/-585 per metric ton <u>and</u> as such it is very much clear that the price fixed by the respondents was the prevalent price of the CDSO <u>and</u> CPO in the international market; that "the Association of the writ petitioners also had a dialogue with the respondents in connection with the fixing the price of the imported goods which would be evident from their letter dated 16-7-1992 (Annexure-2) as such, the allegations of unawareness of the petitioner (sic) <u>and</u> non-disclosure of basis/ source by the respondents are not at all tenanble"; that by letter dated 16-7-1994 (Annexure-2 to the Affidavit-in-opposition) petitioners'' organizations represented to the National Board of Revenue to reconsider the matter of fixation of the value of CDSO circulated through the circular dated 3-7-1994 <u>and</u> that to allow the petitioners to take delivery of the merch<u>and</u>ise imported by them on assessment of customs duties on the basis of tariff value in respect whereof Letters of Credit were opened prior to the deletion of the tariff value <u>and</u> that to have delivery of merch<u>and</u>ise in respect whereof Letters of Credit were opened after deletion of tariff value on assessment of customs duty taking the invoice value as the basis.

53. Petitioners have filed Affidavits-in-Reply to the Affidavits-in-opposition of the respondents No. 2 <u>and</u> 3. In the Affidavit-in-Reply petitioners upon denying the material averments made in the affidavit-in-opposition <u>and</u> reiterating the averments made in the writ petitions have stated, inter alia, that Government is not competent to fix any price like the impugned price <u>and</u> that whatever price is fixed by the Government for the purpose of assessment of customs duties the same is required to be notified through gazette, that the price that has been fixed as ''indicative value'' through the circular dated 3-7-1994 has no nexus to the international market price of the CDSO <u>and</u> CPO, that the circular dated 3-7-1994 being merely internal communication has no legal sanction for assessment of customs duties at a rate different from the invoice value or that higher than the prevalent tariff value; that the price of CDSO as claimed by the respondents to have been obtained being from the countries which are not regular exporting countries <u>and</u> as such, fixation of the price on the basis thereof cannot be considered a dependable basis for fixing the price of CDSO <u>and</u> CPO as fixed through the circular dated 3- 7-1994; that petitioners imported the CDSO <u>and</u> CPO at a price which was quoted by the exporters, that respondents have not obtained the price of CDSO prevalent in the countries is Brazil <u>and</u> Argentina wherefrom petitioners have imported the CDSO <u>and</u> as such, price that has been relied upon in the fixation of price of CDSO as circulated through the circular dated 3-7-1994 has no nexus <u>and</u> bearing in the matter of fixation of the value of CDSO imported by the petitioners; that petitioners opened the Letter of credit prior to the fixation of the ''indicative value'' <u>and</u> as such, ''indicative value'' fixed subsequent to the opening of the Letters of Credit is in no way applicable to the matter of assessment of customs duties of the merch<u>and</u>ise imported by the petitioners.

54. The admitted position is that tariff value of the CDSO <u>and</u> CPO was fixed by the SRO bearing No 214-Law/93 1527/Cus dated 28-10-1993 (Published in the Bangladesh Gazette (Extraordinary) dated 1-11-1993) at US $ 440 per metric ton <u>and</u> at 355 per metric ton respectively <u>and</u> that the tariff value of the said merch<u>and</u>ises were deleted by the SRO XXIV/94/1553/Cus dated 9-6-1994. Respondents fixed ''indicative value'' for the purpose of assessment of customs duty of CDSO <u>and</u> CPO by the circular dated 3-7-1994.

55. Petitioners in Writ Petition Nos 1704 of 1994, 1564 of 1994, 1172 of 1994, 1155 of 1994, 1536 of 1994, 1391 of 1994, 1561 of 1994, 1583 of 1994, 2304 of 1994, 2305 of 1994, 1935 of 1994, 2105 of 1994, 1425 of 1994, 1562 of 1994, 2112 of 1994 <u>and</u> 1163 of 1994 opened the Letters of Credit for import of CDSO <u>and</u> CPO at a period in between the months of April <u>and</u> May, 1994.

56. In the aforementioned writ petitions it is the contention of the Petitioners that they having had opened the Letters of Credit at a time while the tariff value of the merch<u>and</u>ise imported by them was prevalent <u>and</u> as such the customs authority was required to assess the customs duties of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise taking the tariff value that was fixed by the SRO dated 28-10-93 or that the case of declared value is invoice value being higher than the tariff value, then taking the declared value as the basis for assessment of customs duties. As against the aforesaid contention of the petitioner it has been submitted on behalf of the respondents that petitioner having had submitted bills of Entry for the assessment of customs duties of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise at a time when tariff value that was prevalent at the time of opening of the letters of credit was deleted <u>and</u> that thereupon the ''indicative value'' for the purpose of assessment of customs duties was fixed <u>and</u> circulated through the circular dated 3-7-94 <u>and</u> as such, in view of the provisions of section 30 of the Act petitioners'' claim for assessment of customs duties of their imported merch<u>and</u>ise either in the light of the tariff value that was prevalent at the time of opening of the letters of credit or that in the light of the invoice value in case of being higher than the prevalent tariff value at time of the opening of letters of credit is not tenable in law.

57. It has been submitted on behalf of the petitioners that tariff value that was notified through the SRO dated 28-10-1993 having been prevalent at the time when they opened the letters of credit they acquired a vested right to have the customs duties assessed in respect of imported merch<u>and</u>ise in the light of the tariff value <u>and</u> that if in any particular case declared value i e invoice value is higher than the tariff value then at the invoice value. In support of the aforesaid submission the learned Advocate for the petitioners has referred to the decision of the Appellate Division in the Civil Appeal Nos 6-12 of 1995, wherein it has been held that "In the case of Collector of Customs, Chittagong vs. A Hannan (Supra) it has been held that the notification issued under section 19 was without any condition, limitation or restrictions <u>and</u> as such, the subsequent notifications cannot have any operation when a right had vested in the importers <u>and</u> he has acted upon the assurance of the Government in that he would have to pay customs duties at the rate mentioned in the previous notification <u>and</u> as such, a right vested in him could not be taken away. It was nowhere mentioned in the notification that the delivery of the bill of entry will be a determining factor. The decision of the High Court Division in A. Hannan''s case was approved by us in the subsequent case of Ahmed Hossain (Supra) wherein after interpreting sections 19 <u>and</u> 30 of the Customs Act we held that these two reported decisions are on similar lines. This being the legal position, the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellants must succeed."

58. In the aforementioned decision appellants'' (importers) contention of acquiring vested right to have the customs duties assessed on the imported goods taking the tariff value prevalent at the time of opening of the Letters of Credit was accepted. The aforesaid appeals were filed in the background of the facts that the tariff value of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise that was prevalent at the time of opening of the Letter of credit was enhanced by the notifications issued subsequent to the opening of Letter of Credit. After arrival of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise at the port when the petitioners filed import papers for assessment of customs duties, the customs officials took steps for assessment of customs duties in the light of the enhanced tariff value <u>and</u> that for obtaining delivery of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise representation was made to the National Board of Revenue for deduction of tariff value <u>and</u> that having no action taken petitioners moved the High Court Division challenging the legality of the notification enhancing the tariff value <u>and</u> action of the respondents as to assessment of customs duties in the light of the enhanced tariff value that was fixed subsequent to the opening of the Letter of Credit. Writ Petitioners being unsuccessful in the High Court Division went on appeal <u>and</u> obtained leave amongst others "whether by the impugned notification the tariff value could be enhanced giving retrospective effect which was prevalent at a lower rate when respective LCs were opened for importing the said goods which is not only illegal but also affected the vested right of the appellants."

<u>59. Respondents tried to make out a case as to non-application of the principle of law laid down by the Appellate Division in the hereinbefore mentioned appeals upon submitting that in the said appeals the question that came up for consideration was whether assessment of customs duties at the enhanced tariff value notified subsequent to the opening of the Letter of Credit was violative of the importer''s vested right of having his imported goods assessed at the tariff value that was prevalent at the time of opening of the Letter of Credit, but in the instant case question is whether importer (s) has (have) vested right to have his or their imported merch<u>and</u>ise assessed at a tariff value which was prevalent at the time of opening of the Letter of Credit but deleted while the Bills of Entry were submitted for assessment of customs duties. The sole question is whether an importer has vested right to have his merch<u>and</u>ise assessed taking the tariff value which was prevalent at the time of opening of the letter of Credit. This very common question was involved in the hereinbefore mentioned Civil Appeals <u>and</u> that is also involved in the instant Writ Petitions. In the aforesaid state of the matter it is difficult to accept the submission of the learned Attorney-General that the decision in the aforementioned Civil Appeals is not applicable to the instant cases. In the light of the decision in the Civil Appeal Nos 6-12 of 1995 we are of the view that the petitioners of the writ Petitions hereinbefore mentioned or in other words, that said importers have acquired a vested right to have their imported merch<u>and</u>ise assessed in the light of tariff value prevalent at the time of opening of the Letters of Credit. In the background of the law as is at present we are of the view that the action of the respondents in making direction to the petitioners in the hereinbefore mentioned writ petitions to declare the value of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise at a value different from the tariff value that was prevalent at the time of opening of the Letters of Credit or that at a value higher than the declared value or in other words invoice value is not legal. The customs authority is required to assess customs duty of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise of the petitioners in the aforementioned writ petitions taking tariff value that was prevalent at the time of opening of the letters of Credit <u>and</u> that in the cases where declared value or in other words invoice value was higher than the tariff value then taking the declared value as the basis.</u>

<u>60. Now let us come to the question of legality of the price that has been fixed upon coin aging the expression ''indicative value'' by the circular dated 3-7-1994.</u>

<u>61. Learned Advocates of the petitioners has submitted that by the provision of the Act respondents are not authorized to fix normal value or that ''indicative value'' of imported merch<u>and</u>ise at a prior day for the purpose of assessment of customs duties. As against this, it has been submitted on behalf of the respondents that the customs authority is very much authorized or competent to fix at a prior date normal price of that, ''indicative value'' in the light of the provisions of sub-sections (1)(2) <u>and</u> (3) of sections 25 <u>and</u> section 30(1) of the Act. To appreciate the submission made on behalf of the respondents we are reproducing the provisions of sub-sections (1), (2) <u>and</u> (3) of the section 25 <u>and</u> the section 30(1) of the Act below:</u>

<u>"25. Value of imported <u>and</u> exported goods—(1) The value of any imported goods shall be taken to be the normal price, that is to say, the price which they would fetch, on the date referred to in section 30 on a sale in open market between a buyer <u>and</u> a seller independent of each other.</u>

<u>(2) The normal price of any imported goods shall be determined on the following assumption, namely—</u>

<u>(a) that the goods brought by sea or l<u>and</u> are treated as having been delivered to the buyer at the port or place of importation as the case may be <u>and</u> that goods brought by air are treated as having been delivered to the buyer at the airport or place where they are unloaded in Bangladesh, or, if the aircraft first l<u>and</u>s in Bangladesh at some other airport or place without unloading the goods, at such other airport or place;</u>

<u>(b) that the seller will bear freight, insurance commission <u>and</u> all other cost, charges <u>and</u> expenses incidental to the sale <u>and</u> the delivery of the goods at that port, airport or place which will be included in the normal price;</u>

<u>(c) that the buyer will bear any duties or taxes applicable in (Bangladesh) which will not be included in the normal price.</u>

<u>(3) Where the imported goods to be valued—</u>

<u>(a) are manufactured in accordance with any patented invention or are goods to which any protected design has been applied; or</u>

<u>(b) are imported for sale, other disposal or use under a foreign trade mark or are imported for sale, other disposal or use (whether or not after further manufacture) under a foreign trade mark; the normal price shall be determined on the assumption that it includes that value of the right to use the patent, design or trade mark in respect of the goods,</u>

<u>(rest of the provisions are not necessary for the instant cases),</u>

<u>and</u>

30. Date for determination of the value <u>and</u> rate of import duty

(1) The value of <u>and</u> the rate of duty applicable to any imported goods shall be the value <u>and</u> the rate of duty in force:—

<u>(a) in the case of goods cleared for home-consumption under section 79 on the date on which a bill of entry is presented under that section;</u>

(b) in the case of goods cleared from a warehouse for home consumption under section 104, on the date on which the goods are actually removed from the warehouse; <u>and</u>

<u>(c) in the case of any other goods, on the date of payment of duty.</u>

<u>Provided that if a bill of entry is presented in anticipation of arrival of a conveyance by which the goods are imported, the relevant date for the purpose of this section shall be the date on which the manifest of the conveyance is delivered after its arrival;</u>

<u>(Rest of the provisions of the section are not necessary for the instant cases.</u>

62. From a reading of the provision of sections 25(1),(2) (3) <u>and</u> section 30(1) of the Act it is very much seen that if customs authority is authorized to assess customs duties of imported merch<u>and</u>ise at the value prevalent on the date Bill of Entry is presented for assessment of customs duties. The undenied position is that the customs authority fixed the ''indicative value'' for the purpose of assessment of customs duties of the imported CDSO <u>and</u> CPO, the kind of merch<u>and</u>ises imported by the petitioners, much long before the presentation of the Bill of Entry. This being the factual position, the indicative value'' that has been fixed by the circular dated 3-7-1994 cannot be considered to have been fixed in the light of the provisions of the section 25(1), (2) (3) <u>and</u> section 30(1) of the Act.

63. As per provisions of section 25(1), (2) <u>and</u> (3) of the Act the Customs Authority in an appropriate case is no doubt very much competent to fix normal value of imported merch<u>and</u>ise upon rejection of the invoice value or that the declared value. In such a case the customs authority would be required to notify the importer signifying that the customs authority is not accepting the invoice value or declared value as the basis for the purpose of assessment of customs duty <u>and</u> that the said authority is going to fix the normal value of the imported goods for the assessment of customs duties. The customs authority would also be required to afford an opportunity to the importer to place his case, if any, in support of his claim of the invoice value being the normal price of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise for the purpose of assessment of customs duties or that as against the fixation of normal value of imported merch<u>and</u>ise at which the customs authority is going to fix for the purpose of assessment of customs duties. In the instant cases nothing like that has been done by the customs authority. The customs authority fixed through internal circular at certain amount prices of CDSO <u>and</u> CPO for the purpose of assessment of customs duties describing the same as ''indicative value''. Under the Act the Revenue realizing authority or that the customs authority is authorized to fix tariff value under section 25(7) of the Act at a prior date through Gazetted notification for the purpose of assessment of customs duties. The ''indicative value'' that has been fixed <u>and</u> later on circulated through the circular dated 3-7-1994 was admittedly not notified in the official gazette.

64. Learned Attorney-General in the course of his argument submitted that fixation of normal value in every case upon notifying the individual importer would be an impossible task <u>and</u> as such, for the sake of convenience the Revenue authority has fixed the value of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise at a prior date through the circular dated 3-7-1994 for making the same as the basis for assessment of customs duties in disregard of the invoice value. When in fixing the citizen with the liability of payment of tax the concerned authority is required to act in strict compliance of law authorizing it to fix a citizen with the liability of payment of tax, plea of impossibility of fixation of the normal value of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise in the case of each individual importer upon hearing him or that upon affording him an opportunity to place his case, if any, in support of the claim of invoice or declared value of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise as the normal value or that as against the fixation of the value that the customs authority is going to fix for assessment of customs duties as taken by the respondents cannot be accepted <u>and</u> that the respondents in law can not be allowed to resort to the practice of pre-fixation of the value of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise for assessment of customs duties in that Government or that any other agency authorized by the delegated legislation cannot act in a manner which is not authorized or provided in the law or by the law.

65. As regards the correctness or otherwise of the respondents'' contention that the value or in other words ''indicative value'' of the CDSO <u>and</u> CPO that has been fixed <u>and</u> circulated through the circular dated 3-7-1994 for the purpose of assessment of customs duties based on reliable <u>and</u> dependable materials need not be gone into since we have already taken the view that the circular by which price of CDSO <u>and</u> CPO has been fixed has no legal sanction. It may be mentioned that from the Affidavit of the respondents it is not seen that price of the merch<u>and</u>ise in question at which sold by the countries wherefrom import was made was taken into consideration at the time of fixing the'' indicative value''.

66. Petitioners in Writ Petition No.1730 of 1994, 1429 of 1994, 1845 of 1994, 2014 of 1994, 2296 of 1994, 2297 of 1994, 2012 of 1994 <u>and</u> 2015 of 1994 opened their respective Letters of Credit in between July <u>and</u> September, 1994 for import of CDSO <u>and</u> CPO. It has been submitted on behalf of the respondents, since the Letters of Credit were opened by the petitioners of the aforesaid writ petitions after deletion of the tariff value, the customs authority was quite legal in making direction to the petitioners to declare the value of the merch<u>and</u>ise at a value as mentioned in the orders made in the Bills of Entry. The submission made on behalf of the respondents is of no substance since we have already held that in law the revenue authority is not authorized to fix in advance, value of any particular imported merch<u>and</u>ise for the purpose of assessment of customs duty <u>and</u> that to make the same as basis for assessment of customs duty.

67. From the respondents'' side it has been submitted that petitioners'' Associations in their representation dated 16-7-1994 (Annexure 2 to the Affidavit-in-opposition in Writ Petition No.1704 of 1994) admitted that the price of CDSO in the international market at the relevant time was prevalent at about US $ 580/585 per metric ton <u>and</u> in that state of the matter respondents were quite correct in fixing the value of the merch<u>and</u>ise in question at the amount circulated through the circular dated 3-7-1994 for the purpose of assessment of customs duties <u>and</u> as such has committed no illegality in making directions to the petitioners to declare the value of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise at the value as mentioned in the respective orders/directions. Petitioners'' ''Association in its Letter dated 16-7-1994 (Annexure 2 in Affidavit-in-Opposition) addressed to the Member (Customs) of the National Board of Revenue mentioned that in some case import of CDSO has been made at a value at US $ 580/585. In some of the writ petitions it has been stated that the said petitioners have imported some quantity of CDSO at a value in between US 578 <u>and</u> 585 per metric ton <u>and</u> the same has been reflected in the respective invoices. In the light of the aforesaid statement of the petitioner''s Association or that in the background of the value of CDSO shown in some invoices it can in no way be said that invoice value of the respective imports did not reflect the value prevalent in the international market. Be that as it may, fact remains that respondents by law or under the law are not authorized to fix any value like'' indicative value'' by internal circular or any imported merch<u>and</u>ise in advance for the purpose of assessment of customs duties.

68. Learned Advocate for the respondents lastly, has submitted that the matter of assessment of customs duties of the merch<u>and</u>ise in question be sent back to the customs authority for making assessment of customs duties after hearing the petitioners <u>and</u> in support of the said submission has referred to the case of Indus Automoible (Pvt) Limited vs Central Board of Revenue, reported in PLD 1988 Karachi 99. Facts of the reported case are quite distinguishable from the facts of the instant cases. Facts <u>and</u> circumstances in the background whereof the order of rem<u>and</u> was made in the reported case being not present in the instant cases the prayer for sending back the cases to the Customs authority for assessment of customs duties upon hearing the petitioners merits no consideration.

In view of the discussion made above the Rules are made absolute without any order as to costs. The respondents, Customs Authority, are directed to assess the customs duties of the imported merch<u>and</u>ise Letters of Credit whereof were opened prior to the deletion of the tariff value by the SRO dated 9-6-1994 taking the tariff value prevalent at the time of opening of Letters of Credit <u>and</u> that in other cases taking the invoice value. The customs authority is also directed to release Bank Guarantee furnished by the petitioners in the respective writ petitions within 3(three) months from the date of making application attaching the certified copy of the judgment of this court.

End.
